distillation_scope: First-layer disease leaf for the full clinical spectrum of Coccidioides infection. Pulmonary, chronic cavitary, disseminated, meningeal, skeletal, cutaneous, peritoneal, genitourinary, pregnancy-associated, and immunosuppressed-host presentations are represented as mechanisms, axes, risks, or context modifiers, not as disease-name qualifiers.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Airborne Coccidioides arthroconidia from endemic soil are inhaled and convert to tissue spherules in terminal bronchioles or lung parenchyma. The exposure can be recent or remote, and the pulmonary focus may be mild, occult, or clinically dominant.

Impaired or insufficient cell-mediated containment of Coccidioides spherules permits higher pulmonary burden, relapse, or lymphohematogenous spread. Pregnancy, advanced HIV, solid organ transplant, glucocorticoids, TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, diabetes, older age, and high-risk ancestry modulate this activity.

Viable Coccidioides spherules and endospores in lung parenchyma, pleura, or regional nodes. This drives pulmonary symptoms, necrotizing granulomas, serologic response, and the reservoir for chronic or disseminated disease.

Macrophage, Th1, IL-6, TNF, eosinophilic, and granulomatous response to spherules. It produces fever, fatigue, CRP/ESR elevation, eosinophilia, thrombocytosis, erythema nodosum, arthralgia, and constitutional symptoms.

Necrotizing granulomatous pneumonia, airspace consolidation, nodules, pleural inflammation, effusion, or empyema physiology from pulmonary coccidioidomycosis. Severity ranges from mild pneumonia-like illness to hypoxemic respiratory failure.
Persistent granulomatous remodeling after pulmonary infection creates nodules, thin- or thick-walled cavities, fibrocavitary disease, fungal ball, hemoptysis, pneumothorax, or bronchopleural fistula.

Spherules or endospores spread beyond lung and pleura through lymphatics or blood to meninges, bone, joints, skin, soft tissue, peritoneum, genitourinary tract, liver, adrenal glands, eye, or other organs.

Basilar or diffuse meningeal infection causes lymphocytic or eosinophilic meningitis, headache, nausea, cranial neuropathy, hydrocephalus, vasculitis, stroke, arachnoiditis, and high relapse risk without lifelong suppression.

Coccidioides seeding of vertebrae, pelvis, ribs, long bones, joints, or adjacent soft tissues causes lytic lesions, osteomyelitis, arthritis, pathologic fracture, epidural abscess, draining sinus, or malignancy-like masses.

Hematogenous or direct tissue infection produces papules, plaques, nodules, ulcers, abscesses, draining sinuses, verrucous lesions, alopecia-like plaques, or cellulitis-like soft tissue disease containing spherules.

Less common dissemination to peritoneum, omentum, bowel, kidney, prostate, epididymis, adrenal glands, liver, or other viscera. It can mimic malignancy, tuberculosis, bacterial abscess, or inflammatory bowel disease.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Treatment delay, inadequate coverage, or relapse activity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Ongoing viable burden and tissue damage from delayed diagnosis, inactive or poorly absorbed antifungal therapy, nonadherence, drug interaction, relapse after stopping therapy, or inadequate source control.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Inhaled arthroconidia mature into spherules in pulmonary tissue.
Weaker Th1/macrophage containment permits higher viable fungal burden.
Dissemination is enriched in pregnancy, immunosuppression, diabetes, and high-risk ancestry, reflecting impaired containment.
Spherule antigen burden drives granulomatous and systemic inflammatory response.
Pulmonary fungal burden and host response produce pneumonia, pleuritis, and necrotizing granulomas.
Persistent pulmonary foci remodel into nodules or cavities over weeks to months.
The pulmonary focus is the usual reservoir for lymphatic or hematogenous seeding.
Fever is common in symptomatic acute pulmonary or disseminated coccidioidomycosis.
Granulomatous and cytokine activity elevates CRP, though values vary widely.
ESR often rises in pulmonary, skeletal, or chronic coccidioidal disease.
Peripheral eosinophilia is a useful inflammatory clue and can be striking in disseminated disease.
Erythema nodosum is an immune-mediated reactive eruption of acute coccidioidal infection rather than direct skin invasion.
Fatigue can be prominent and prolonged even when pulmonary findings are modest.
Pulmonary coccidioidomycosis commonly presents as cough resembling community-acquired pneumonia.
Pulmonary consolidation, pleural effusion, diffuse disease, or rupture can produce dyspnea.
Pleural inflammation and effusion produce pleuritic pain.
Airspace disease, consolidation, nodular infiltrates, or diffuse pneumonia are typical radiographic pathways.
Pleural involvement can create exudative effusion or empyema-like presentations.
Extensive pulmonary disease reduces oxygenation.
Nodules may persist and mimic malignancy.
Pulmonary cavities are a classic chronic pulmonary complication.
Cavities, fungal balls, or superinfection may cause hemoptysis.
Meningitis is a common severe site of dissemination.
Bone and joint disease can emerge months after an unrecognized pulmonary infection.
Skin and soft tissue are frequent extrapulmonary dissemination sites.
Rare visceral, peritoneal, or GU involvement occurs through the same dissemination pathway.
Headache is the dominant presenting symptom of coccidioidal meningitis.
Meningeal inflammation and intracranial pressure can produce nausea and vomiting.
CSF pleocytosis is typically lymphocytic and may include eosinophils.
Meningeal inflammation raises CSF protein.
Fungal meningitis can lower CSF glucose, though early or treated cases may be near-normal.
CNS mechanism directly defines the daily risk of clinically consequential coccidioidal meningitis.
Skeletal coccidioidomycosis commonly produces destructive lytic lesions or osteomyelitis.
Bone and joint lesions commonly present with localized pain, swelling, or mass effect.
Destructive lytic lesions can fracture through weakened bone.
Direct cutaneous dissemination can form nodules, ulcers, abscesses, plaques, or draining sinuses.
Peritoneal coccidioidomycosis can produce ascites and omental inflammation.
Granulomatous peritoneal or omental disease can mimic carcinomatosis or tuberculosis.
Renal parenchymal abscess is rare but documented as disseminated coccidioidal GU disease.
Inactive therapy, poor absorption, or nonadherence allows viable burden to persist or recur.
Delayed or inadequate therapy is especially dangerous in meningitis, severe pulmonary disease, and immunosuppressed hosts.

axes.display_name: Cutaneous ulcer, nodule, plaque, or draining sinus

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and CRP share upstream inflammatory activity but can diverge in immunosuppressed hosts.
More extensive pulmonary or pleural disease lowers oxygen saturation.
Large effusions can cause dyspnea independent of parenchymal infiltrate.
Hypoxemia from severe pulmonary coccidioidomycosis or ARDS raises short-term mortality.
Basilar meningitis can obstruct CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus.
Untreated hydrocephalus and high intracranial pressure are major mortality pathways.
Coccidioidal meningitis is a high-mortality complication without sustained effective therapy.
Expansile destructive lesions weaken bone and raise fracture risk.
Epidural abscess can cause cord compression, sepsis-like deterioration, or surgical emergencies.
Peritoneal disease often requires paracentesis, biopsy, or operative sampling to distinguish malignancy/TB and manage ascites.
Severe amphotericin nephrotoxicity or electrolyte derangement can worsen outcome, particularly in prolonged therapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: High-dose fluconazole has CSF penetration and is used for long-term suppression in coccidioidal meningitis.
Clinically significant hepatotoxicity or interactions may require alternate azole, dose adjustment, or amphotericin bridge.

side_effects.interpretation: Transaminitis, cholestasis, QT/drug interaction risk; monitor liver enzymes and interactions.

treatments.context_specific_role: Oral azole backbone for symptomatic pulmonary disease needing treatment, disseminated non-CNS disease, and long-term or lifelong CNS suppression.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Itraconazole has strong clinical use for osseous and soft-tissue coccidioidomycosis when absorption and drug levels are adequate.
Itraconazole is less useful for meningeal disease than high-dose fluconazole or salvage azoles with CNS strategy.

side_effects.interpretation: Hepatotoxicity, negative inotropy, CYP3A4 interactions; therapeutic drug monitoring matters.

treatments.context_specific_role: Useful for bone, joint, and soft-tissue disease when drug exposure can be assured.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Amphotericin is the systemic option when azoles are avoided in early pregnancy or severe pregnancy-associated disease.
Renal toxicity and electrolyte wasting limit duration or require lipid formulation and close monitoring.

side_effects.interpretation: Renal vasoconstriction and tubular toxicity with electrolyte wasting.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid induction for severe pulmonary disease, rapidly progressive dissemination, pregnancy-associated severe disease, or azole failure before step-down therapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Used when fluconazole is not controlling CNS or disseminated disease, with drug level and toxicity monitoring.
Extended-spectrum azoles add hepatic, QT, visual, neurotoxicity, and interaction risks.

side_effects.interpretation: Hepatotoxicity, QT effects, photosensitivity or neurovisual toxicity depending on agent.

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative azole pathway for refractory, intolerant, or relapsing disease after reassessing diagnosis, exposure, interactions, and source control.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Large abscesses, destructive bone disease, empyema, spinal compression, or diagnostic tissue needs require procedural management.

side_effects.interpretation: Successful procedure reduces mechanical burden but does not replace antifungal therapy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct for drainable abscess, empyema/ruptured cavity, spinal epidural abscess, unstable skeletal lesion, or diagnostic tissue acquisition.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hydrocephalus or high opening pressure may need CSF diversion or repeated drainage in addition to antifungal therapy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct for high intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus; does not control the fungal mechanism by itself.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pregnancy-associated immune state cannot be reduced like iatrogenic immunosuppression; antifungal selection changes instead.

side_effects.interpretation: Clinical tradeoff is allograft rejection or autoimmune flare risk rather than direct fungal toxicity.

treatments.context_specific_role: Consider in transplant, TNF inhibitor, JAK inhibitor, steroid, or other iatrogenic immunosuppression after balancing the underlying condition.
Exposure management for itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, interaction-heavy regimens, long courses, relapse, or toxicity.

risk_factors.factor: Residence, travel, or occupational dust exposure in an endemic area

endemic_soil_exposure.trajectory_modulation: Raises prior probability through inhaled arthroconidia exposure; construction, agriculture, excavation, dust storm, military training, or travel can be sufficient.

no_known_endemic_exposure.trajectory_modulation: Does not exclude disease because remote residence, unrecognized travel, and expanding endemicity occur.

african_or_filipino_ancestry.trajectory_modulation: Higher risk of dissemination and severe disease after infection.

pregnant_or_postpartum.treatment_effect_modulation: Early pregnancy shifts systemic therapy toward amphotericin when treatment is required; azole teratogenicity context matters.

risk_factors.factor: Advanced HIV or severe T-cell lymphopenia
Solid organ transplant or high-intensity iatrogenic immunosuppression

present.treatment_effect_modulation: Reduction of immunosuppression can strengthen containment but may threaten graft or underlying disease control.

risk_factors.factor: TNF inhibitor, JAK inhibitor, or chronic glucocorticoid exposure

age_over_65.trajectory_modulation: Higher risk of severe pulmonary disease and treatment complications.

male.trajectory_modulation: Male sex is associated with higher dissemination risk in epidemiologic series.

risk_factors.factor: Delayed diagnosis, inactive antifungal coverage, nonadherence, or drug interaction

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises persistence, relapse, tissue destruction, and dissemination burden.

supportive_care: Do not use culture, PCR, histopathology, or serology as ordinary presentation-ranking evidence; keep them as confirmatory/context evidence.
Assess endemic residence, remote travel, dust exposure, construction/agricultural work, incarceration, military desert training, and prior valley fever history.
Track fever curve, respiratory symptoms, oxygenation, chest imaging, CRP/ESR, eosinophils, CBC, liver enzymes, renal function, and symptoms suggesting dissemination.
Perform lumbar puncture when headache, persistent nausea/vomiting, meningismus, cranial neuropathy, altered mental status, or other CNS signs appear; monitor opening pressure and hydrocephalus.
Evaluate focal bone pain, joint swelling, draining sinus, or soft tissue mass with targeted imaging and tissue diagnosis when safe.
For abscess, empyema, ruptured cavity, epidural abscess, or unstable bone lesion, coordinate procedural source control with antifungal therapy.
Monitor azole liver enzymes, QT risk, drug interactions, adherence, and therapeutic levels when using itraconazole, voriconazole, or posaconazole.
Monitor amphotericin renal function, potassium, magnesium, infusion reactions, and volume status; use lipid formulation when toxicity risk is high.
In pregnancy or early postpartum disease, coordinate infectious disease, maternal-fetal medicine, and neonatology; antifungal selection depends on gestational timing and severity.
In transplant or biologic-treated patients, coordinate immunosuppression reduction with the treating specialty to balance fungal control and graft or disease flare risk.
For coccidioidal meningitis, plan long-term or lifelong suppressive azole therapy and monitor for relapse, hydrocephalus, arachnoiditis, vasculitis, and cranial neuropathy.
Follow complement fixation titers and imaging as longitudinal context, not as standalone ranking observations.
